attachment.cliPrefix: You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- courier:changeset-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when you need changeset@2 artifacts produced from a git diff. Input is a git diff, optionally a linked spec@1, and optionally smith's criteria_evidence from the TDD run that produced this diff. A diff spanning multiple independent topics produces one changeset@2 per topic, never one bundled entry — see judgment for how topics are distinguished. For each topic, classifies consumer_impact (behavior-change, new-capability, internal-only) and semver_impact (major, minor, patch, none) per shared/references/delivery/changesets.md's decision table, identifies that topic's own changed files, detects breaking changes, and maps acceptance_criteria IDs. Uses smith's criteria_evidence directly when supplied; otherwise reconstructs best-effort file-level evidence from the diff. Summary detail scales with semver_impact — terse for patch/internal-only, full old-to-new-to-required-action detail for major. Output is one or more changeset@2 objects conforming to shared/schemas/changeset@2.json, routed to pr-narrator or release-summarizer. (Tools: All tools)

- courier:commit-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when the user has staged git changes and needs a conventional commit message written. Input is the staged diff. The agent reads shared/references/delivery/commits.md for type and scope conventions. Output is a JSON object containing commit_message, type (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci, or build), scope (or null), a breaking flag, and a reasoning scratchpad. The commit message explains why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed. The reasoning field is a private scratchpad explaining type and scope selection; it is not forwarded downstream. (Tools: All tools)

- courier:pr-narrator: Delegate to this subagent when the user needs a pull request title and body written for a set of staged or committed changes. Input is a git diff and optionally a linked spec@1 or requirement@1. The agent reads the PR template from shared/references/delivery/github.md and writes from the reviewer's perspective — what does a reviewer with zero prior context need to know to approve this confidently? Output is a JSON object with title, body, labels, and a reasoning scratchpad. The body covers what changed, why it was needed, and how to verify correctness. It explains the change's purpose, not a summary of the diff. Labels are inferred from the change type. (Tools: All tools)

- courier:release-summarizer: Delegate to this subagent when you need a release-artifact@2 generated from a collection of changeset@2 entries. Input is a list of changeset@2 JSON objects, the prior released version string, and a release date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Each input changeset already carries consumer_impact and semver_impact, set at authoring time by changeset-analyzer — this agent does not re-derive them. It filters out consumer_impact: internal-only entries, computes the release version as max(semver_impact) across the remaining changesets applied to the prior version, and carries each changeset's summary through as-is (already written in consumer-facing language at the right detail level). All breaking_changes strings from all input changesets are aggregated into the top-level breaking_changes array. Output is a release-artifact@2 conforming to shared/schemas/release-artifact@2.json. (Tools: All tools)

- courier:review-preprocessor: Delegate to this subagent before a PR is opened, to assemble the complete review package for the reviewer. Input is the changeset diff, optionally a linked spec@1 or requirement@1, test results, and any open questions the author wants answered. The agent bundles these into a structured review package — diff summary, linked spec reference, test result summary, and open questions list — so the reviewer has everything in one place before they start. Mechanical assembly only; no judgment about the change. Output is a JSON object with diff_summary, linked_spec, test_results, open_questions, and a reasoning scratchpad. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- mason:auditor: Delegate to this subagent to audit a plugin directory for ecosystem conformance. Check manifests, declared files, agent structure, prompt-prefix identity, routing, contracts, instruction economy, runtime reference quality, and shared linkage. Use repository validators for deterministic checks. Treat length as a review signal; fail prose only with evidence of filler, repetition, mixed rules, unsupported absolutes, or missing refutation. Read-only. Return a structured report. (Tools: All tools)

- mason:evaluation-adjudicator: Independently compare a completed isolated workflow run with its hidden fixture oracle and live evidence. Return `harness-evaluation@2` without prose scoring. (Tools: All tools)
- mason:evaluation-runner: Run one fixed behavioral fixture in an isolated workspace without reading its answer key. Return `evaluation-run@1` for independent adjudication. (Tools: All tools)

- mason:scaffolder: Delegate when creating a plugin or adding one agent to an existing plugin. Generate conformant manifests, skills, agents, routing, and shared linkage for the requested scope. Copy the constitution byte-for-byte. Return a JSON report of created files. (Tools: All tools)

- mason:schema-designer: Delegate to this subagent when the user wants to design a new JSON Schema for an inter-agent artifact — a structured payload passed between producers and consumers in the plugin ecosystem. Provide a description of what the artifact represents, who produces it, and who consumes it. The designer produces a JSON Schema following ecosystem conventions (draft 2020-12, $id as name@version, all fields documented, reasoning scratchpad field always present, additionalProperties false, required fields listed), checks for conflicts with existing schemas in shared/schemas/, and returns the schema object with a recommended filename. (Tools: All tools)

- muse:auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need adversarial quality review of a component spec@1 before it enters planning. Input is a spec@1 JSON object describing a UI component. Checks for completeness: missing interactive states (hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), missing accessibility criteria (role, name, focus order, keyboard operability, live-region or state-announcement behavior), invalid prop combinations not marked as error cases, ambiguous phrasing, scope overlap with other component specs, and unnecessary prose that costs every downstream reader without adding a needed fact. For every issue, produces the rewritten fix, not just a description. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix) and an overall pass/fail verdict. Standard: can a developer implement this component without one clarifying question? Does not check the spec against source artifacts — that's a verification concern; this checks whether the spec, on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable. (Tools: All tools)

- muse:drafter: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 (or free-text design intent) and need a formal component spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 and optionally design references (mockup description, existing component family, design-system tokens). Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json: id (SPEC-NNN), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), optional api_surface for the component's props. Every criterion must be falsifiable — confirmable by a tester with no implementation knowledge, using only observable behavior: rendered output, focus order, ARIA attributes, emitted events. Props, variants, every interactive state (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), and accessibility criteria are each named explicitly. Error cases and invalid prop combinations carry is_error_case: true. Unknowns go in non_goals or reasoning — no TBDs anywhere. The muse orchestrator writes the spec to disk after exit-gate passes; this agent returns the spec object only. Also runs in correction mode: given spec_file_path, a criterion_id, and implementer's contradiction report, revises the affected criterion (and any dependent ones) and returns the full corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. (Tools: All tools)

- muse:exit-gate: Delegate to this subagent when a component spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before entering the planning phase. Input is a spec@1 JSON object describing a UI component. This is an adversarial gatekeeper — the default disposition is fail, and the spec must earn a pass. The spec passes only if all four conditions hold: every acceptance criterion is a testable proposition with no vague language, no TBDs remain anywhere in the document, error cases and invalid prop combinations are explicitly covered with is_error_case: true criteria, and every interactive state and accessibility criterion (role, name, focus order, keyboard operability) implied by the component's props is present. On fail, every blocker is specific enough for the drafter to make a targeted fix without further clarification. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json with artifact_type set to spec@1. This agent is the binding exit gate — its fail verdict halts progression to navigator until the spec is corrected and resubmitted. Maximum 3 retries before escalation to a human reviewer. (Tools: All tools)

- navigator:challenger: Delegate to this subagent when a plan@1 needs adversarial review before implementation. Input is a plan@1 and its source spec@1. Check missing work, dependency order, prescription, batching, error handling, criterion coverage, and interface siblings against live evidence. Return per-issue repairs and a binding pass or fail verdict. (Tools: All tools)

- navigator:estimator: Delegate to this subagent when a plan@1 exists and you need a rough effort estimate before committing to execution. Input is a plan@1 JSON object. The agent produces a per-task time estimate in minutes, marks each task as parallelizable or sequential, lists blocking dependencies by task ID, and produces a total_minutes sum with explicit assumptions. The implementer is assumed to have full codebase context but no domain knowledge of the feature being built. A task is marked parallelizable only if it has no dependency on any other task in the current plan. All assumptions affecting the estimate are listed explicitly in an assumptions array. Output is a JSON object with total_minutes, a tasks array, and assumptions. (Tools: All tools)

- navigator:planner: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed spec@1 and need a sequenced, executable implementation plan. Input is a spec@1 (or its spec_file_path, read from disk if provided). Output is a plan@1 conforming to shared/schemas/plan@1.json, with spec_file_path and spec_hash propagated from the spec. Decomposes into dependency-ordered tasks (foundational types, then logic, then integration); each task includes exact file paths, a brief implementation approach, exact implementation code as a concrete baseline (smith's implementer may improve on its shape, not its scope), the exact tests proving each criterion it covers, the verification command, a commit message, and covers_criteria naming every acceptance criterion it addresses. Every criterion must appear in some task's covers_criteria. Each task is one independently reviewable unit of change, sized to its Subsystem Batch's compilation boundary rather than a clock-time estimate; no TBDs. Also runs in amend mode: given an existing plan@1, a corrected spec@1, and the changed criterion_ids, patches only the affected tasks (adding new ones for newly introduced criteria) and leaves the rest untouched. Route output to challenger. (Tools: All tools)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- ranger:adversary: Invoke once per candidate after scanner and, for T7 or T10, boundary tracing. Try to refute reachability from current code and return `candidate-assessment@1`. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:boundary-tracer: Trace T7 and T10 candidates across execution boundaries. Supports Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Go. Return `field-survival-map@1`. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:exit-gate: Independently verify remediated `finding-report@2` entries and their defect families against current code. Return `verdict@3`. (Tools: All tools)

- ranger:recon: Invoke before scanning. Detect affected languages, trace reachable files from live entry points, and inventory project capabilities and current workspace state. Return `workspace-manifest@1`; do not judge defects. (Tools: All tools)

- ranger:scanner: Invoke after recon. Load the hazard pack for each scoped language, scan only live files, and emit every matching `candidate@1` without verdicting. Supports Rust, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, and Go. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:arch-auditor: Delegate to this subagent when a draft spec@1 needs checking against the workspace's whole-system architecture before it enters scribe/gate-spec — not against another spec, and not against a single function's signature, but against module boundaries, canonical abstractions, and invariants that span the codebase. Input is a spec@1 draft plus workspace_root. Default (check) mode: reads the persisted arch-model@2 at docs/architecture/model.json (or notes it is absent), reads broadly enough across the workspace to confirm the model still reflects reality, and checks the spec against it — flagging boundary violations (a dependency running the wrong direction), competing abstractions (a new type reinventing something the model already canonicalizes), and invariant conflicts. Output is an arch-audit@1 conforming to shared/schemas/arch-audit@1.json. Build mode: given no usable model or an explicit refresh request, reads the codebase broadly and produces or updates an arch-model@2 conforming to shared/schemas/arch-model@2.json — module boundaries, canonical abstractions, and invariants (each citing its governing decision record when one exists), the latter cumulative across everything scribe/architect has ever fixed. This agent does not patch specs or code — it reports fit, or builds the model fit is checked against. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:architect: Delegate when `finding-report@2`, `implementation-review@2`, or `implementation-result@1` identifies a structural defect class. Inspect the live semantic model and persisted architecture, then produce a `spec@1` that makes recurrence impossible or machine-detectable. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need adversarial quality review of a spec@1 before it enters planning. Input is a spec@1 JSON object. Checks seven dimensions: untestable/vague criteria, ambiguous phrasing, missing error cases, scope overlap with other specs, TBDs/incomplete sections, unnecessary prose that costs every downstream reader without adding a needed fact, and a field this spec introduces or changes on a type that another spec persists, serializes, or transmits with no matching round-trip criterion on the far side and no note that the gap is intentional. For every issue, produces the rewritten fix, not just a description. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix) and an overall pass/fail verdict. Standard: can a developer implement this spec without one clarifying question? Does not check the spec against source artifacts — that's verifier's role; this checks whether the spec, on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:drafter: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 and need a formal spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 and optionally a research-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json: id (SPEC-NNN), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), optional api_surface. Every criterion must be falsifiable — confirmable by a tester with no implementation knowledge, using only observable behavior. Error cases carry is_error_case: true. Unknowns go in non_goals or reasoning — no TBDs anywhere. The scribe orchestrator writes the spec to disk after exit-gate passes; this agent returns the spec object only. Also runs in correction mode: given spec_file_path, a criterion_id, and implementer's contradiction report, revises the affected criterion (and any dependent ones) and returns the full corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:drift-checker: On-demand diagnostic: given a spec_file_path and a workspace root, verifies the current code still implements every acceptance criterion in the spec. Reads the spec from disk, not from context, and reads implementation/tests from the workspace. When a prior changeset@2's criteria_evidence is available, uses its pointers as a starting point but re-verifies each one — code may have moved since it was recorded. Classifies each criterion as covered (implementation and tests match the contract), uncovered (nothing found), or drifted (behavior diverges from the criterion). Not a blocking gate — exit-gate is. Use for ongoing maintenance, detecting drift weeks or months after implementation. Output is a drift report with covered/uncovered/drifted arrays plus a summary. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:exit-gate: Issue the binding `verdict@3` for a `spec@1` before planning. Pass only when every criterion is testable, error behavior is explicit, no TBD remains, scope fits one planning cycle, and all checks are complete. (Tools: All tools)

- scribe:verifier: Delegate to this subagent when you need to verify that a draft spec@1 is grounded in its source artifacts — the requirement@1 and optional research-report@1 — before it proceeds to auditing or gating. Input is a spec@1 draft plus the originating requirement@1 and any research-report@1 used to produce it. For each acceptance criterion, the agent checks whether the requirement or research report supplies evidence that the criterion is necessary and correctly scoped. Each criterion is classified as supported (evidence found with a direct citation), unsupported (criterion appears with no basis in the source artifacts), or overfitted (criterion is narrower than the source supports, excluding valid cases). The agent collects evidence only and does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Output is a structured evidence report with supported, unsupported, and overfitted arrays plus a reasoning scratchpad. For post-implementation drift checking, use drift-checker instead. (Tools: All tools)
- sentinel:exit-gate: Issue `verdict@3` from a completed verification report. Separate blockers, coverage gaps, and pending checks; pass only within the verified scope. (Tools: All tools)

- sentinel:recon: Delegate to this subagent at the start of the sentinel gate protocol when an artifact must be inventoried before verification begins. Input is an artifact path or description. The agent determines the artifact type, locates it in the workspace, enumerates the criteria it must be verified against (derived from a linked spec or requirement, or from the artifact's own acceptance criteria section if none is linked), and identifies source files to cross-check during verification. This is purely mechanical discovery — the agent produces no pass/fail opinion. Output is a JSON manifest with artifact_type, artifact_path, criteria array, source_files array, and a reasoning scratchpad. Do not delegate here for judgment; route the manifest to verifier for criterion cross-reference. (Tools: All tools)

- sentinel:verifier: Delegate to this subagent after recon has produced its artifact manifest, and before any final verdict is issued. Input is the recon manifest from recon, including the artifact path, criteria list, and source files. The agent reads the artifact and each source file and, for each criterion, collects concrete evidence that confirms or refutes it. Each criterion is classified as verified (positive evidence found), failed (evidence contradicts the criterion), or unverifiable (requires external context not accessible). Absence of a counter-example is not sufficient to classify a criterion as verified. This agent is a neutral evidence collector — it does not issue verdicts. Output is a JSON object with verified, failed, and unverifiable arrays. Route output to exit-gate for the final verdict. (Tools: All tools)

- smith:exit-gate: Delegate after all planned batches have terminal results and approved `implementation-review@2` artifacts. Verify current code, scoped evidence, sibling completeness, and pending work independently. Return `verdict@3`. (Tools: All tools)

- smith:implementer: Delegate to execute one plan task. Read persisted criteria, design and implement the change, prove it with tests, and record exact evidence. Commit only when the caller supplies `commit_authorized: true`; otherwise return a null commit SHA. Report spec contradictions or architecture needs instead of forcing a pass. Scope is one task. (Tools: All tools)

- smith:mutator: Delegate after implementation. Use available project-native mutation tooling against changed behavior, or a controlled deliberate fault when appropriate. Analyze survivors and return `mutation-report@2`; unavailable tooling becomes a coverage gap. (Tools: All tools)

- smith:recon: Delegate before implementation. Inspect current workspace state, affected languages, entry points, project-native verification capabilities, baseline tests, and persisted artifact freshness. Return `workspace-manifest@1`; stop on a failing baseline. (Tools: All tools)

- smith:reviewer: Delegate after an implementation batch and discrimination check. Review scope, verification fit, related defects, semantic models, and architecture. Return `implementation-review@2`; route structural families to `scribe:architect`. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vanguard:reader: Delegate to this subagent after recon produces a source map. Input is the source map from recon plus the original research question. The agent reads every identified source and extracts findings relevant to the question, with a citation, confidence level (confirmed, likely, or assumed), and source attribution for each. Does not synthesize or recommend — extracts faithfully from what it reads. Sources that cannot be read are noted as unreadable rather than skipped. The agent maps where answers might live — existing specs, docs, manifests, codebase patterns, or external sources — and returns a structured research agenda that tells reader exactly which sources to read. Does not read file contents; relevance is assessed from names and directory structure only. Output is a JSON object containing internal_sources, external_keywords, existing_implementations, scope, and a reasoning scratchpad. Input is a proposed approach or research-report@1 JSON, optionally accompanied by context about the target environment. The agent identifies technical risks that would materially affect the spec or plan if left unaddressed. For each risk it produces a description, severity (critical, high, medium, or low), likelihood, a concrete trigger condition describing when the risk materializes, and a mitigation sketch. Only risks with a plausible failure path are included — theoretical concerns without a realistic trigger are excluded. Output is a JSON object with a prioritized risks array and an overall_risk assessment. Surfaces risks neutrally — no recommendation about whether to proceed. (Tools: All tools)

- vanguard:synthesizer: Delegate to this subagent after reader produces a findings list. Input is the findings array and reasoning from reader, along with the original research question. The agent synthesizes findings into a coherent research-report@1, surfaces contradictions between sources, identifies patterns across findings, and lists open questions that remain unanswered. Output is a complete research-report@1 conforming to shared/schemas/research-report@1.json. The recommendation includes an explicit confidence level (high, medium, or low), the rationale, a list of open questions, and any contradictions called out explicitly. - weaver:auditor: Delegate to this subagent to cross-reference open requirements against existing specs, persisted plans, and implementation files. Input is a list of open requirement@1 objects. - weaver:intake: Delegate to this subagent when you have a raw need statement in free text — a problem description, user story, or feature request — and need it converted into a structured requirement@1 draft. Input is unstructured text only; no schema is required from the caller. The agent infers id, statement, stakeholder, why, and done_when from the provided text without asking any clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted; gaps are noted in the reasoning scratchpad. The out_of_scope field is intentionally left empty — populating it is the clarifier's responsibility. Output is a flat requirement@1 JSON object conforming to shared/schemas/requirement@1.json. Every done_when criterion must be a testable proposition verifiable from outside the implementation. Output is an ordered list with a stated rationale per requirement, plus any dependency relationships found. Does not modify requirement@1 objects — ranking and rationale only. (Tools: All tools)

Never asks multiple questions at once — one question per invocation. Output is a JSON object with action (question or complete), question (or null), the current requirement, and reasoning. When action is complete, out_of_scope is populated with explicit scope boundaries. Route completed requirements to drafter. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:intake: Delegate to this subagent when you have a raw need statement in free text — a problem description, user story, or feature request — and need it converted into a structured requirement@1 draft. Input is unstructured text only; no schema is required from the caller. The agent infers id, statement, stakeholder, why, and done_when from the provided text without asking any clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted; gaps are noted in the reasoning scratchpad. The out_of_scope field is intentionally left empty — populating it is the clarifier's responsibility. Output is a flat requirement@1 JSON object conforming to shared/schemas/requirement@1.json. Every done_when criterion must be a testable proposition verifiable from outside the implementation. Route this output directly to clarifier before writing a spec. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:prioritizer: Delegate to this subagent when a set of requirement@1 drafts needs ranking before planning starts. Input is a list of requirement@1 objects. The agent ranks them by impact (who is affected and how badly), urgency (signals in why/done_when indicating time pressure), and dependency order (a requirement that another depends on ranks above the one depending on it, regardless of its own impact/urgency score). Output is an ordered list with a stated rationale per requirement, plus any dependency relationships found. Does not modify requirement@1 objects — ranking and rationale only. (Tools: All tools)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

## Latest MCP Specification Version

The current protocol version is 2026-07-28. This specification includes a stateless protocol core, the Extensions framework, Tasks, MCP Apps, authorization hardening, and a formal deprecation policy.

## Key Features of the Latest Version

The 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification replaces legacy stateful constraints with a fully stateless core, enabling cloud-native horizontal scaling, serverless deployments, and standard round-robin load balancing.

## Key Concepts

**Skills**: A skill is typically a SKILL.md file plus optional scripts, references, and assets. Skills are for reusable workflows and domain expertise, and remain the authoring format while plugins are the installable distribution unit.

**Plugins**: Plugins are distributable bundles of skills + apps + MCP servers.

**Subagents**: Subagents were announced in general availability for OpenAI Codex, after several weeks of preview behind a feature flag.

**Custom Agents**: Codex lets you define custom agents as TOML files in ~/.codex/agents/, which can have custom instructions and be assigned to use specific models.

**TOML Configuration**: Multi-agent settings and custom role declarations are configured through a config.toml table.

**Hooks**: Lifecycle hooks can be enabled and loaded from hooks.json or inline [hooks] config. Hooks are now stable and configurable inline in config.toml and requirements.toml.

# Google Antigravity Plugin Format

## Manifest File

Every plugin requires a **`plugin.json`** file at its root. The minimal structure includes:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://antigravity.google/schemas/v1/plugin.json",
  "name": "my-custom-plugin",
  "description": "Brief description of functionality"
}
```

The `name` field must match the pattern `^[a-zA-Z0-9-_]+$` and is required for CLI management.

## Directory Layout

Plugins follow this optional structure:

```
plugins/<plugin-name>/
├── plugin.json          # Required manifest
├── mcp_config.json      # Optional MCP servers
├── hooks.json           # Optional lifecycle hooks
├── skills/              # Optional skill definitions
├── agents/              # Optional subagent templates
└── rules/               # Optional behavioral rules
```

## Supported Components

According to the documentation, plugins can contain "skills, background subagents, linting rules, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and lifecycle hooks."

## Installation Commands

The CLI provides plugin management via `agy plugin`:

```bash
# Install from marketplace
agy plugin install <name>@antigravity-plugins-official

# Install from GitHub or local path
agy plugin install https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>
agy plugin install </path/to/plugin>

# Manage plugins
agy plugin list [--json]
agy plugin enable/disable/uninstall <name>
```

## Platform Compatibility

These plugins work across **Antigravity App**, **CLI**, and **IDE** with cross-surface synchronization. However, the documentation contains **no information** about compatibility with Claude or Codex plugin formats.

# Key Changes in the 2026-07-28 MCP Specification

**Stateless Protocol Core**
The most significant change transforms MCP from a bidirectional stateful protocol into a stateless request/response model. As noted, "Every request is self-describing, with an optional discovery call for clients that want capabilities up front, so any request can land on any instance behind a plain round-robin load balancer."

**Header-Based Routing**
Method and tool names now travel in HTTP headers (`Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name`), enabling gateways to route and authorize without parsing JSON bodies.

**Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR)**
This replaces server-initiated requests that previously required open streams. Servers can now return `resultType: "input_required"` with needed responses, allowing clients to retry with answers attached—enabling mid-call confirmations and parameter collection over stateless connections.

**Tasks Extension**
Tasks graduated from experimental status into the formal extensions framework, featuring poll-based retrieval and update capabilities alongside a unified subscription system.

**Caching and Authorization**
List responses now include cache hints (`ttlMs`, `cacheScope`) for improved performance. Authorization evolved to include RFC 9207 issuer validation and a shift from Dynamic Client Registration toward Client ID Metadata Documents.

**Formal Extensions Framework**
MCP Apps and Enterprise Managed Authorization join Tasks within an official extensions structure, establishing clearer governance for protocol evolution.

**Deprecations**
Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated with a twelve-month minimum support window, establishing predictable upgrade pathways.

# Subagents in ChatGPT and Codex

Subagents enable parallel agent workflows by spawning specialized agents that handle independent tasks simultaneously, then consolidating results into a single response.

## Key Capabilities

**Core functionality**: ChatGPT Work and Codex can delegate parallel work to multiple agents, keeping the main thread focused on requirements while subagents handle exploration, testing, and analysis tasks in the background.

**Why this matters**: Subagent workflows prevent "context pollution"—where noisy intermediate output buries important information—by moving verbose work off the main conversation thread.

## Triggering Workflows

- **ChatGPT Work**: At most intelligence levels, explicitly request subagents. Ultra mode enables proactive delegation.
- **Codex (local)**: Direct requests or applicable `AGENTS.md`/skill instructions trigger delegation.
- **Codex (CLI)**: Use `/subagents` command to switch between threads while agents run.
- **Codex (IDE)**: Background-agent panel displays active subagent status.

## Configuration

**Global settings** in `config.toml` under `[agents]`:
- `enabled` (boolean) — toggles multi-agent tools
- `max_concurrent_threads_per_session` — limits concurrent agent threads
- `default_subagent_model` — sets default model for spawned agents
- `default_subagent_reasoning_effort` — configures reasoning depth

**Custom agent files** (`.codex/agents/` or `~/.codex/agents/`) require three fields: `name`, `description`, and `developer_instructions`. Optional fields control model selection and disable specific capabilities.

## Built-in Agents

Codex includes three default agents: `default` (general-purpose), `worker` (execution-focused), and `explorer` (read-heavy exploration).

## Model & Reasoning Selection

Start with `gpt-6.1-sol` for complex reasoning tasks or `gpt-6-luna` for faster, narrowly scoped work. Reasoning effort levels (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `ultra`) balance intelligence versus speed and token consumption.

I found detailed information about Codex plugins, marketplace.json, and the .codex-plugin format. Here's what I found:

## Plugin Structure

The only required file in a Codex plugin is .codex-plugin/plugin.json. Plugins typically include optional components such as skills in a skills/ directory, .app.json for app integrations, .mcp.json for MCP server config, and assets like icons and logos.

## marketplace.json Format

A marketplace is a JSON manifest (marketplace.json) that declares available plugins, their sources, and installation policies. Marketplace files should be placed at the repo-level ($REPO/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json) or personal level (~/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json).

## Plugin Installation

You can install plugins from configured marketplaces by name using commands like `codex plugin add codex-security` or specify a version like `codex plugin add codex-security@1.2.0`. When a user installs a plugin, Codex copies it into a cache at ~/.codex/plugins/cache/$MARKETPLACE_NAME/$PLUGIN_NAME/$VERSION/, with $VERSION being "local" for local plugins.

## Plugin Format Compatibility

Codex supports multiple plugin formats: .agents/plugins/marketplace.json (Codex marketplace), .claude-plugin/marketplace.json (Claude-compatible marketplace), .claude-plugin/plugin.json (standalone Claude plugin), and native plugins can reference .codex-plugin/plugin.json along with Claude-compatible plugins and Agent Plugins 1.0 packages.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Gemini 3, Antigravity, browser subagent capabilities, and artifact verification:

## Browser Subagent Capabilities

The Antigravity browser subagent can open a real Chrome window, navigate to running apps, click buttons, fill forms, take screenshots, and loop back to fix issues. The subagent has access to tools for controlling the browser including clicking, scrolling, typing, reading console logs, and can read open pages through DOM capture, screenshots, or markdown parsing, as well as taking videos.

## Screenshots and Recordings

The browser subagent can take screenshots of open pages or elements when it needs review of the page state, and all screenshots are saved as image artifacts that can be commented on. Antigravity operates on browser tabs capturing screenshots and saving action videos as interactive artifacts.

## Artifacts for Verification

When modifying UI code, the agent will build and run the app and capture a screenshot of the updated UI as an Artifact, which you'll see in the Agent Manager as that screenshot or a short walkthrough video. Artifacts are tangible deliverables like task lists, implementation plans, screenshots, and browser recordings that allow you to verify the agent's logic at a glance.

## UI Verification Process

When requesting UI changes like "Make the signup button green and slightly larger," the agent modifies the UI code, then builds and runs the app and captures a screenshot of the updated UI as an Artifact.

## Cursor 3 Launch and Architecture

Cursor 3 launched April 2, 2026 with a new Agents Window, Design Mode, and cloud agents. The team rebuilt the interface from scratch around a new idea: that most code will be written by AI agents, and the developer's job is to orchestrate them, not write every line.

## Design Mode and Browser

Design Mode lets you annotate and select UI elements directly in the Agents Window's built-in browser. You can drag-select areas and add elements to agent conversations via keyboard shortcuts, giving the agent precise visual context about what to change. Design Mode allows developers to select UI elements and describe desired changes in natural language, with AI agents automatically implementing the modifications.

## Agents and Parallel Execution

The new Agents Window enables developers to run many agents in parallel across local, cloud, worktree, and remote SSH environments — all managed from a unified sidebar. If you used the Cursor 1.x background-agents and 2.x multitask-style flows, 3.0 is the version where this stopped being a novelty and became the primary surface.

## Bugbot

Bugbot (graduated to fixer, Feb 2026) reviews PRs and, when it finds a real bug, spins up its own cloud agent, tests a fix, and proposes it directly on the PR. Resolution rate now around 80% — meaningfully ahead of competing review bots.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Agent Plugins 1.0 specification:

## Overview

Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for packaging reusable components into portable plugins, with version 1.0.0 specification defining a shared format for Agent Skills and MCP servers that compatible clients can discover and load consistently.

## Release and Adoption

On August 6, 2026, OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, Cursor, and Vercel jointly launched Agent Plugins 1.0.0, aiming to establish a universal plugin packaging format for AI Agents. ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Kiro, and VS Code support it at launch.

## Package Structure

A plugin is a folder with a required plugin.json manifest, an optional skills/ folder of Agent Skills, and an optional mcp.json declaring MCP servers. According to version 1.0.0 specification, an Agent Plugin is a directory with a fixed structure, and the root directory must contain plugin.json, with the minimal manifest only needing to declare the adopted specification version and the plugin name.

## Scope and Purpose

The format standardizes AI agent plugin packaging for cross-product use, allowing developers to build one package for multiple clients such as ChatGPT, Codex, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot. Agent Plugins does not replace Agent Skills or MCP. It packages them without changing their native formats.

## Current Status

The 1.0.0 specification is still labeled as a "working draft," currently standardizing only the packaging method without defining plugin marketplaces, installation protocols, permission models, sandbox isolation, or source verification.

I found several relevant benchmarks and research papers for evaluating front-end UI generation agents. Here are the key findings:

## Major 2026 Benchmarks

Vision2Web systematically evaluates multimodal coding agents across static webpage generation, interactive frontend development, and full-stack website construction, with a focus on the multimodal nature of web engineering, where an agent must translate visual designs into functional, responsive, and interactive systems.

VISTA turns design handoffs into application-construction tasks that require integrated frontend, backend, and database implementations across 18 applications. The benchmark includes 8,487 human-annotated components defining reference locations, interaction types, and navigation targets; the evaluator checks each against the running application, yielding localization and behavior scores.

## Evaluation Approaches

Traditional evaluation approaches largely rely on static artifacts such as rendered screenshots or source code, but agent-based evaluators operate in two modes: for pass rate, acting as an informed expert, and for usability, simulating a naive user exploring the site.

Visual evaluation follows metrics from Design2Code, comparing the visual output of generated code to the ground-truth screenshot, focusing on layout accuracy, content fidelity, and stylistic alignment.

## Recent Benchmarks Include

Multiple benchmarks have been developed including Code-Vision (2025) for evaluating multimodal LLMs' logic understanding and code generation capabilities for frontend and visual-interactive tasks, along with other frameworks like WebUIBench, FrontendBench, and specialized benchmarks for interactive webpage generation.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Agent Skills and related standards:

## Agent Skills Overview

Agent Skills is an open standard for packaging procedural knowledge, instructions, scripts, and resources into portable directories that artificial intelligence agents can discover and load dynamically to perform specialized tasks. Originally developed within Anthropic's Claude Code as an internal feature in October 2025, the format was released as a vendor-neutral open standard on December 18, 2025, with a published specification and reference software development kit hosted at agentskills.io.

## Adoption and Ecosystem Growth

The format had been adopted by more than sixteen major commercial tools and dozens of open-source projects, establishing it as a de facto standard for portable agent behavior specifications by mid-2026. The standard was released by Anthropic on December 18, 2025, and was adopted with remarkable speed: within 48 hours Microsoft had wired it into VS Code via Copilot and OpenAI had added it to ChatGPT and Codex. By March 2026 more than 30 tools from competing companies were reading the same SKILL.md files.

## Relationship with AGENTS.md and Agentic AI Foundation

Launched in August 2025, AGENTS.md provides project-specific context. Over 60,000 open-source projects have adopted this format for communicating build instructions, architectural decisions, and coding conventions to AI assistants. In December 2025, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). This organization provides neutral governance ensuring these standards evolve through community consensus rather than vendor control.

The broader agentic AI ecosystem, including related standards like MCP and AGENTS.md, is coordinated through the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, whose platinum members include AWS, Anthropic, Block, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

# Agent Plugins Specification Summary

**Manifest & Structure:**
The spec requires `plugin.json` to identify plugins and target version. Directory layout includes: `skills/` for Agent Skills components, `mcp.json` for MCP servers, and reverse-domain namespaces like `com.example.client/` for client-specific extensions.

**Included Components:**
- Agent Skills (per Agent Skills specification)
- MCP servers (stdio, Streamable HTTP, or legacy HTTP+SSE)
- Skills contain SKILL.md documentation, scripts, and references
- Client-specific hooks and behaviors in extension namespaces

# Vision2Web: Evaluated Models and Key Findings

## Models Evaluated

The benchmark tested several state-of-the-art vision-language models:
- Claude-Opus-4.5
- Gemini-3-Pro-Preview
- Various Qwen iterations
- GLM-4.6V (for GUI verification)

## Key Results

**Performance by Complexity Level:**
Claude-Opus-4.5 demonstrated the strongest overall performance, achieving "a VS of 58.9 on desktop webpages and maintaining a FS of 57.6 on full-stack tasks." However, a dramatic decline occurs across task difficulty levels, with models struggling significantly more as requirements shift from static pages to interactive and full-stack development.

**Form Factor Challenge:**
Models consistently underperformed on mobile and tablet layouts, with visual scores typically dropping 10-20% for smaller resolutions, indicating difficulty with "the denser, more vertically oriented layouts" of mobile design.

## Visual Verification Findings

The workflow-based verification paradigm employed two complementary approaches:

1. **Visual Verification Nodes:** A VLM judge performed "component-level comparison between the rendered page and the original prototype," assigning fidelity scores based on layout, color, and content accuracy.

2. **Failure Patterns:** Even at the simplest level, agents struggled with "precise alignment of repeating components" and accurate color reproduction, revealing fundamental challenges in visual-to-code translation.

# VISTA: Visual Spec-to-Web-App Coding Benchmark

**VISTA** is an end-to-end benchmark that evaluates coding agents' ability to convert design mockups into functional applications. The research addresses a critical gap: "a screen that looks right is not an application that works."

## Key Findings

The benchmark tested 14 deployed coding-agent systems with these results:
- **Web applications**: Best joint score of 0.553
- **Mobile (Android)**: Best joint score of 0.378
- **Behavioral gap**: 13 of 14 systems performed worse on behavior than localization for Web

## Dataset Overview

VISTA includes 8,487 human-annotated interactive components across:
- 126 Web pages
- 576 Android screens
- 18 total applications

## Notable Observations

Development traces revealed concerning patterns in agent workflows:
- 44.5% of trajectories never examined design screenshots
- 73.0% skipped prescribed self-audits
- 8.3% reported success despite failed checks

Component probes detected unresponsive controls in 90.1% of audited Web deliveries, highlighting substantial gaps between visual design completion and functional implementation.

The research demonstrates that existing metrics focusing on visual reconstruction alone inadequately measure application quality.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Codex hooks, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop hooks, and hooks.json:

## Overview

Codex CLI runs hooks on 12 lifecycle events, from PreToolUse to Interrupt. As of 2026-06, lifecycle hooks are part of current Codex builds and are enabled by default. In April 2026 (v0.124.0), hooks were promoted to stable.

## Key Hook Events

PreToolUse fires before a tool runs and can block execution, PostToolUse fires after tool completes, and Stop fires when the agent's turn ends. PreToolUse fires before Codex executes a tool call and receives the tool name and full command, so you can inspect it, approve it, or deny it outright. PostToolUse fires after a tool call finishes and receives the tool name, the command, and the output, allowing you to replace the tool result with feedback that steers the agent's next move.

## Configuration (hooks.json)

Hooks run scripts or MCP tools during the agentic loop, loaded from hooks.json files or inline [hooks] tables in config.toml. Inline [hooks.*] tables in config.toml and requirements.toml are now supported in addition to hooks.json.

## Hook Input/Output

Each hook is a shell command (or an MCP tool call) that receives a JSON payload on stdin and can answer with JSON on stdout. PreToolUse and PermissionRequest accept a hookSpecificOutput JSON envelope.

# Plugin Packaging Guide Summary

## Core Manifest Structure

A portable plugin requires `plugin.json` at its root. The manifest declaration includes:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json",
  "name": "my-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Plugin description"
}
```

The plugin name should use kebab-case format and serves as the stable identifier across hosting platforms.

## Directory Layout

Standard plugin structure includes:
- **plugin.json** - Portable manifest (required)
- **skills/** - Workflow definitions (optional)
- **mcp.json** - MCP server configuration (optional)
- **assets/** - Visual resources like icons and logos
- **.codex-plugin/plugin.json** - Compatibility overlay (legacy support)

## OpenAI-Specific Metadata

Add platform-specific details via `extensions.com.openai`:

> "Put OpenAI-specific presentation, registered MCP server mappings, and hook settings under `extensions.com.openai` in root `plugin.json`."

This includes display names, descriptions, icons, category tags, and capability declarations.

## Skills Integration

To include workflows, create `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` with front matter defining the skill's name and purpose, followed by implementation instructions.

## MCP Server Configuration

Remote servers use this structure in `mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/mcp.schema.json",
  "mcpServers": {
    "server-name": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://example.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

## Authentication Options

MCP servers support several auth methods via `extensions["com.openai"].auth`:
- None
- OAuth (with provided clients, DCR, or CIMD)
- API key
- Mixed (public + OAuth)

## Local Testing & Distribution

**Repo marketplace**: Place `marketplace.json` at `$REPO_ROOT/.agents/plugins/`

**Personal marketplace**: Use `~/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`

Marketplace entries point to plugin directories and control discovery in the ChatGPT desktop app.

## Publishing Options

- **Local/repo**: Use marketplace files for team distribution
- **Workspace**: Workspace admins can publish to team boundaries
- **Public**: Submit through the official portal for universal directory listing

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the OpenAI Agents SDK 2026 update:

## Core Features

The SDK ships four first-class primitives: handoffs, output_type, input/output guardrails, and hosted tracing.

## Sandbox Agents

Sandboxing Python places agents in controlled computer environments where they are siloed within a designated workspace, with only permitted files and code accessible, solving the core enterprise risk of agents running unsupervised with broad system access. Sandbox agents support manifest-defined files, sandbox client selection, and resumable sandbox sessions.

## Handoffs

Agents support agent-to-agent task delegation with full handoffs and 'Agents as Tools' patterns where agents are called like functions.

## Guardrails

Guardrails provide input and output validation with lightweight checks that enforce safety policies, content rules, and formatting requirements across the workflow.

## Tracing

Tracing automatically records the full execution graph — tool calls, handoffs, model outputs — with no extra instrumentation required. Model calls, tool calls, handoffs, and guardrails are recorded as spans you can inspect in the OpenAI Traces dashboard.

## Latest Release

The OpenAI Agents SDK is available for Python (openai-agents 0.24.0, released October 15, 2026) and TypeScript (@openai/agents 0.20.0, released October 8, 2026).

## Responses API Integration

The SDK uses the Responses API by default for OpenAI models, but it wraps model calls in a higher-level runtime.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the A2A protocol and related technologies:

## A2A Protocol (Agent2Agent)

The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) is an open standard for communication between independent agents, originated by Google, which lets one agent discover another's capabilities through an Agent Card, exchange messages, delegate tasks, and receive artifacts across vendor and framework boundaries. A2A reached v1.0 in March 2026 and joined the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation in August 2026.

## Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)

It's important to note that there are **two different protocols abbreviated as "ACP"**:

1. **IBM's Agent Communication Protocol**: IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, which addressed agent-to-agent communication, became part of A2A under the Linux Foundation in August 2025.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SKILL.md portability across Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor:

## Core Portability

Skills are portable in format but not in install path: Claude Code reads .claude/skills/, Codex reads .agents/skills/, and Antigravity reads ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/.

## Frontmatter Portability Issues

Claude Code adds disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, context: fork (run the skill in an isolated subagent), argument-hint, paths, model, hooks and more, but Claude Code-only frontmatter gives you allowed-tools, model overrides, argument hinting, paths-based auto-loading, isolated subagent contexts. None of it survives porting.

## Specific Non-Portable Features

Features that don't port include: context: fork (runs skill in an isolated subagent), agent: Explore (specifies which subagent type to use), !`command` (dynamic context injection), allowed-tools (pre-approves tools without permission prompts), and model and effort (overrides session model).

Additionally, hooks (event-driven triggers) are supported by Claude Code only. Other agents ignore hooks.

## What Works Across Agents

The most reliable approach: stick to name, description, when_to_use in your frontmatter, and write instructions in plain markdown. Avoid agent-specific fields unless you're building exclusively for one platform.

# OpenAI Astra: Autonomy Duration and Long-Run Support

## Claimed Duration
OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra averages "roughly 40 minutes per task" on the OSWorld 2.0 offline subset, with a 72.6% success rate on that benchmark.

## Features Supporting Long Runs
The article does not identify any built-in Astra features specifically designed for extended autonomy. Instead, it emphasizes that **the model itself lacks native mechanisms** for surviving infrastructure failures during multi-hour tasks.

The author argues that durability must be implemented at the application layer through:
- **Step-based checkpointing**: Breaking tasks into named steps with persistent state
- **Graceful shutdown handling**: Resuming from the last completed step when processes restart
- **Idempotency keys**: Preventing duplicate effects when steps replay

## Important Caveats
The article stresses several limitations:

1. **High failure rates on agentic tasks**: Astra's 72.6% success score means roughly one in four attempts fail—expensive when each run consumes thousands of tokens over 40 minutes.

2. **No protection against replayed side effects**: Checkpointing prevents redundant computation but doesn't prevent duplicate API calls unless downstream systems implement idempotency.

3. **Infrastructure mismatches**: HTTP timeouts, Kubernetes deployments, serverless duration limits, and connection drops all remain threats to long runs regardless of model capability.

## Adobe Spectrum Agent Skills & MCP

Agent Skills function as a specialized playbook that gives AI the exact rules, format, and boundaries to do one job perfectly. The Skill holds the business logic and tells the AI what to build and how to structure it, then points the AI to the MCP server to get the specific code needed to execute it.

Adobe's Spectrum Design Data includes a Model Context Protocol server providing AI assistants with structured access to Spectrum design system data, along with a Design Data Agent MCP server distinct for AI agent authoring sessions. Adobe also offers a Design Data Skill as a packaged Claude Code agent skill for consuming Spectrum design data from agent sessions.

## GitHub Primer & Design System Integration

GitHub offers a "github-primer-brand" skill for designing GitHub-branded marketing surfaces with @primer/react-brand. Additionally, the GitHub MCP server provides AI agents with programmatic access to GitHub's API through the Model Context Protocol.

## Design System AI-Ready Distribution in 2026

Making tokens, components, and patterns consumable by AI coding tools involves three pillars: machine-readable tokens, MCP servers, and component contracts agents can actually use. Using the Model Context Protocol, modern platforms allow AI agents to "understand" design systems, enabling agents to generate tickets, code, and documentation in real-time that are 100% on-system.

The teams shipping fastest in 2026 share three things: tokens an agent can parse without rendering anything, components with prop shapes the agent can't violate without a type error, and a query surface (usually MCP) the agent can hit during a session.

Tags: [P] primary page read, [S] search summary only, [U] unverified. Several vendor pages returned 403; secondary blogs are [S].

## 1. Capabilities table
| Harness | Capability | Source + tag | Implication for plugin repo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Codex | Skills = SKILL.md folders (.agents/skills); plugins are the install unit bundling skills, MCP, apps, hooks, browser extensions | learn.chatgpt.com/docs/plugins [P]; codemyspec.com/blog/skill-portability [S] | Skills are the shared authoring unit; Codex counterpart can be near 1:1 |
| Codex | Plugin build: portable root plugin.json (Agent Plugins schema), OpenAI-only data under extensions.com.openai; legacy .codex-plugin/plugin.json overlay; marketplace at $REPO/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json | developers.openai.com/plugins/build/plugins [P] | Matches repo's generated .agents/plugins layout; migrate generator toward portable plugin.json + overlay |
| Codex | Reads Claude-format marketplaces (.claude-plugin/*) reportedly | codex.danielvaughan.com plugin-marketplace posts [S] | Verify before dropping the Codex generator; do not rely on it |
| Codex | Custom agents: TOML in .codex/agents/ or ~/.codex/agents/; required name, description, developer_instructions; optional model/effort/disabled capabilities; built-ins default/worker/explorer; [agents] max_concurrent_threads_per_session, default_subagent_model, default_subagent_reasoning_effort | learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents [P] | Markdown role cards must compile to TOML; model tier maps to model/effort fields |
| Codex | Subagents spawn on explicit request or when AGENTS.md/skill says so; CLI /subagents; IDE background-agent panel | same [P] | Orchestrator skills must say "spawn agent X" explicitly; no automatic dispatch |
| Codex | Hooks stable since v0.124 (Apr 2026), ~12 events incl. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop; hooks.json or inline [hooks] in config.toml/requirements.toml | danielvaughan.com hooks guide, turboai hooks docs [S] | Binding gates can be mechanically enforced via a Stop hook on Codex; Claude hooks need a counterpart |
| Codex | Managed git worktree tools (CLI 0.162.0, 2026-10-08); Command Center task pinning; /daemon; parallel read-only tools (0.163.0, 10-15) | learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog [P] | Worktree isolation for parallel agents is native |
| Codex | Browser: sandboxed in-app browser; Chrome extension (2026-05-07) with per-thread tab groups, DevTools, authenticated sessions; Computer Use in desktop app | macrumors.com/2026/05/07/openai-codex-chrome-extension; thenewstack.io [S] | Visual verification native on Codex; skills should name the capability, not the tool |
| Codex | Models: GPT-6.1 Sol default since 2026-09-29; Luna fast/narrow; Astra top tier; effort low/medium/high/ultra (Luna to max); GPT-5.5 retired 10-14; Sol Ultrafast 10-08 | changelog [P]; subagents doc [P] | Tier map: haiku/low -> Luna, sonnet/med -> Sol medium, opus/high -> Sol high/ultra or Astra |
| Codex | Autonomy: OpenAI says GPT-6 handles tasks spanning hours or days; Astra about 40 min/task on OSWorld 2.0 (72.6%); no-CoT 50% horizon about 31 min (UK AISI) | openai.com/index/practical-guide-building-gpt-6 [S, page 403]; dev.to Astra article [P]; lesswrong [S] | Long-run claims are vendor claims; gates must not assume uninterrupted runs; keep durable artifacts on disk |
| Codex | Guardian safety reviews, Code Mode, Instant Interrupt, Multi-agent V2 (also on Bedrock) | changelog [P] | Runtime-level review exists; do not duplicate |
| OpenAI SDK | Agents SDK (py 0.24.0 2026-10-15; TS 0.20.0): handoffs, agents-as-tools, input/output guardrails, tracing spans, sandbox agents with manifest files + resumable sessions; Responses API default | openai.github.io/openai-agents-python; developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sandboxes [S] | Role cards + schema-first handoffs map to handoffs + output_type; usable as an eval harness |
| Antigravity (AGY) | Plugins: required plugin.json ($schema antigravity.google/schemas/v1/plugin.json, name), optional mcp_config.json, hooks.json, skills/, agents/, rules/; no Workflows | antigravity.google/docs/plugins [P] | Repo's AGY plugin shape is close; verify hooks/mcp filenames against our layout |
| AGY | `agy plugin install <name>@antigravity-plugins-official`, GitHub URL or local path; marketplace UI + /plugin; third-party marketplace.json schema NOT in public docs | antigravity.google/docs/marketplace [P] | Marketplace schema reference is a verification gap/risk |
| AGY | Antigravity 2.0 (I/O May 2026): desktop app with Manager, CLI (Go), SDK; dynamic subagents on Gemini 3.5 Flash; Artifacts (task lists, plans, screenshots, recordings) | cybernews.com, tosea.ai [S] | Artifacts are native evidence objects; our evidence schema should be attachable as AGY artifacts |
| AGY | Browser subagent: real Chrome, click/type/console/DOM, screenshots + videos saved as commentable artifacts | antigravity.google/docs/ide/browser, /screenshots [S] | Native visual verification; scripting capture is redundant here |
| AGY | Gemini CLI retired 2026-06-18; extensions import as plugins; reads GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md | developers.googleblog.com transition post [S] | Drop a separate Gemini CLI extension target |
| AGY | Workflows stop working 2026-10-19 | search summary of Google docs [S] | Do not author workflows; skills only |
| Cursor | Cursor 3 (2026-04-02): Agents Window, parallel local/cloud/worktree/SSH agents, Design Mode in built-in browser; Bugbot ~80% resolution claim; Cursor co-authored Agent Plugins 1.0 | medium/dev.to reviews [S]; agent-plugins.org [P] | Design Mode is human-in-loop element selection; complements spec gates |
| GitHub Copilot | Coding agent reads AGENTS.md; custom agents as .github/agents/*.agent.md; skills in CLI/VS Code/coding agent; Agent Plugins support | github.blog changelog 2025-08-28 [S]; devleader.ca [S] | Another markdown role-card format; same compile-from-role-card approach |
| Kiro / Amp / Warp / Windsurf / JetBrains Air | Kiro: specs, steering, hooks, skills, powers; Amp: Oracle subagent; Warp: Oz cloud orchestration; Windsurf Cascade; Air details not found | augmentcode.com, builder.aws.com [S]; Air [U] | Reach via AGENTS.md + SKILL.md only; no bespoke targets |

## 2. Standards state
- Agent Skills: open since 2025-12-18, 16+ tools by mid-2026 [S].
- AGENTS.md: 60k+ repos; governed with MCP under AAIF (Linux Foundation, Dec 2025) [S].
- Agent Plugins 1.0.0 (2026-08-06) by Amazon, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, Vercel: plugin.json + skills/ + mcp.json + reverse-domain extension namespaces. Explicitly excludes hooks, commands, agents, marketplaces, permissions, trust. Working draft. Clients: ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, VS Code [P: agent-plugins.org, aaif.io/blog/from-skills-and-tools-to-portable-agent-plugins]. Claude Code and AGY not named as adopters.
- MCP 2026-07-28 [P: blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28]: stateless core, Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers, Multi Round-Trip Requests (input_required, replaces server-initiated elicitation streams), Tasks extension (poll-based), MCP Apps in Extensions framework, cache hints, CIMD auth; Roots, Sampling, Logging deprecated (12-month window).
- A2A v1.0 (Mar 2026), joined AAIF Aug 2026 [S]. Zed Agent Client Protocol (editor-to-agent) distinct and active [S]. llms.txt not researched [U].

## 3. Evals on front-end / visual verification
- VISTA (arXiv 2605.26144) [P abstract]: 14 deployed agent systems; best web joint score 0.553, Android 0.378; 44.5% of trajectories never examined design screenshots; 73.0% skipped prescribed self-audits; 8.3% reported success despite failed checks; unresponsive controls in 90.1% of audited web deliveries.
- Vision2Web (arXiv 2603.26648) [P]: Claude-Opus-4.5 best (58.9 visual score desktop; 57.6 full-stack); mobile/tablet 10-20% lower; weak at aligning repeated components and color.
- Also 1D-Bench, FronTalk, EvoGenUI-Bench, ProgramDistill [S, unread]. No head-to-head Claude Code vs Codex vs AGY UI eval found; do not claim one.

## 4. Portability analysis
Survives: SKILL.md body, name/description, references/scripts directories, MCP servers, AGENTS.md prose, JSON Schemas (ours, harness-neutral), Agent Plugins core.
Does not survive [S: codemyspec.com, agensi.io]: Claude frontmatter (allowed-tools, model, effort, context: fork, agent:, hooks, dynamic command injection), skill-level hooks (other agents ignore them), install paths (.claude/skills vs .agents/skills vs ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills), subagent definition format (md vs TOML vs .agent.md), workflows, marketplace schema. Agent Plugins deliberately omits hooks/agents/marketplaces, which is exactly what our repo depends on, so those stay per-harness.
Ship-once precedents: shadcn ships 10 skills over Figma + shadcn MCP for Claude/Cursor/Codex/OpenCode [S]; Salesforce SLDS ships an MCP toolset + 3 first-party skills with bundled JSON registries via npm [S]; Adobe Spectrum ships design-data MCP + a skill [S]; Primer evidence thin [U]. Pattern: knowledge lives in MCP/data registries, thin SKILL.md on top, no per-harness agent logic.
Enforcement differs: Codex and Claude hooks can make gates binding; Cursor/Copilot/AGY gate by prose and artifacts only. Binding judgment should therefore live in a schema-validated verdict artifact checked by a script.

## 5. What each harness natively does that our plugins re-implement
- Parallel subagents + worktrees (Codex, Cursor 3, AGY Manager): keep only the handoff contract, not dispatch prose.
- Browser/screenshot/recording capture (Codex Chrome ext + in-app browser, AGY browser subagent, Cursor browser): specify required evidence, let the harness capture.
- Plan/task-list artifacts (AGY Artifacts): plan@1 is analogous; make attachable.
- Review/fix loops (Bugbot, Codex Guardian): do not rebuild.
- Spec-driven workflow (Kiro specs/steering): overlaps scribe/navigator; ours differs via falsifiable criteria and binding gates.
- Tracing/guardrails/handoffs (Agents SDK): our verdict/handoff schemas are the portable analog.
Not found natively anywhere: falsifiable-criterion specs, adversarial refutation, fail-by-default binding gates, enforced self-audit (VISTA shows agents skip it). That is the differentiator.

## 6. Standards to adopt
1. Agent Plugins 1.0 portable plugin.json as manifest core, vendor data under reverse-domain extensions; keep generated Codex overlay until verified redundant.
2. Restrict portable SKILL.md frontmatter to name/description (+ when_to_use); move Claude-only fields to overlay.
3. AGENTS.md canonical; CLAUDE.md/GEMINI.md thin pointers.
4. MCP 2026-07-28 for any server we ship: stateless, Tasks for long checks, MRTR instead of elicitation, MCP Apps optional for verdict UI; avoid Sampling/Roots/Logging.
5. Keep JSON Schema handoffs ours; A2A Agent Card only if cross-vendor calls appear.
6. Add a capability-matrix check: skills declare required capabilities (browser, subagent, hook); generator fails if a target lacks one.
7. Anti-VISTA gate rule: no pass without screenshot/evidence refs and an executed self-audit.

## Gaps
Cursor and Copilot specifics are secondary-source only; JetBrains Air, llms.txt, Primer, Windsurf, Warp not verified; AGY marketplace.json schema undocumented publicly; Codex loading .claude-plugin formats unverified on a primary page; GPT-6 multi-hour autonomy figures are vendor claims I could not read (openai.com 403).

## 2. Standards state
- Agent Skills: open since 2025-12-18, 16+ tools by mid-2026 [S].
- AGENTS.md: 60k+ repos; governed with MCP under AAIF (Linux Foundation, Dec 2025) [S].
- Agent Plugins 1.0.0 (2026-08-06) by Amazon, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, Vercel: plugin.json + skills/ + mcp.json + reverse-domain extension namespaces. Explicitly excludes hooks, commands, agents, marketplaces, permissions, trust. Working draft. Clients: ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, VS Code [P: agent-plugins.org, aaif.io/blog/from-skills-and-tools-to-portable-agent-plugins]. Claude Code and AGY not named as adopters.
- MCP 2026-07-28 [P: blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28]: stateless core, Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers, Multi Round-Trip Requests (input_required, replaces server-initiated elicitation streams), Tasks extension (poll-based), MCP Apps in Extensions framework, cache hints, CIMD auth; Roots, Sampling, Logging deprecated (12-month window).
- A2A v1.0 (Mar 2026), joined AAIF Aug 2026 [S]. Zed Agent Client Protocol (editor-to-agent) distinct and active [S]. llms.txt not researched [U].

## 3. Evals on front-end / visual verification
- VISTA (arXiv 2605.26144) [P abstract]: 14 deployed agent systems; best web joint score 0.553, Android 0.378; 44.5% of trajectories never examined design screenshots; 73.0% skipped prescribed self-audits; 8.3% reported success despite failed checks; unresponsive controls in 90.1% of audited web deliveries.
- Vision2Web (arXiv 2603.26648) [P]: Claude-Opus-4.5 best (58.9 visual score desktop; 57.6 full-stack); mobile/tablet 10-20% lower; weak at aligning repeated components and color.
- Also 1D-Bench, FronTalk, EvoGenUI-Bench, ProgramDistill [S, unread]. No head-to-head Claude Code vs Codex vs AGY UI eval found; do not claim one.

## 4. Portability analysis
Survives: SKILL.md body, name/description, references/scripts directories, MCP servers, AGENTS.md prose, JSON Schemas (ours, harness-neutral), Agent Plugins core.
Does not survive [S: codemyspec.com, agensi.io]: Claude frontmatter (allowed-tools, model, effort, context: fork, agent:, hooks, dynamic command injection), skill-level hooks (other agents ignore them), install paths (.claude/skills vs .agents/skills vs ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills), subagent definition format (md vs TOML vs .agent.md), workflows, marketplace schema. Agent Plugins deliberately omits hooks/agents/marketplaces, which is exactly what our repo depends on, so those stay per-harness.
Ship-once precedents: shadcn ships 10 skills over Figma + shadcn MCP for Claude/Cursor/Codex/OpenCode [S]; Salesforce SLDS ships an MCP toolset + 3 first-party skills with bundled JSON registries via npm [S]; Adobe Spectrum ships design-data MCP + a skill [S]; Primer evidence thin [U]. Pattern: knowledge lives in MCP/data registries, thin SKILL.md on top, no per-harness agent logic.
Enforcement differs: Codex and Claude hooks can make gates binding; Cursor/Copilot/AGY gate by prose and artifacts only. Binding judgment should therefore live in a schema-validated verdict artifact checked by a script.

## 5. What each harness natively does that our plugins re-implement
- Parallel subagents + worktrees (Codex, Cursor 3, AGY Manager): keep only the handoff contract, not dispatch prose.
- Browser/screenshot/recording capture (Codex Chrome ext + in-app browser, AGY browser subagent, Cursor browser): specify required evidence, let the harness capture.
- Plan/task-list artifacts (AGY Artifacts): plan@1 is analogous; make attachable.
- Review/fix loops (Bugbot, Codex Guardian): do not rebuild.
- Spec-driven workflow (Kiro specs/steering): overlaps scribe/navigator; ours differs via falsifiable criteria and binding gates.
- Tracing/guardrails/handoffs (Agents SDK): our verdict/handoff schemas are the portable analog.
Not found natively anywhere: falsifiable-criterion specs, adversarial refutation, fail-by-default binding gates, enforced self-audit (VISTA shows agents skip it). That is the differentiator.

## 6. Standards to adopt
1. Agent Plugins 1.0 portable plugin.json as manifest core, vendor data under reverse-domain extensions; keep generated Codex overlay until verified redundant.
2. Restrict portable SKILL.md frontmatter to name/description (+ when_to_use); move Claude-only fields to overlay.
3. AGENTS.md canonical; CLAUDE.md/GEMINI.md thin pointers.
4. MCP 2026-07-28 for any server we ship: stateless, Tasks for long checks, MRTR instead of elicitation, MCP Apps optional for verdict UI; avoid Sampling/Roots/Logging.
5. Keep JSON Schema handoffs ours; A2A Agent Card only if cross-vendor calls appear.
6. Add a capability-matrix check: skills declare required capabilities (browser, subagent, hook); generator fails if a target lacks one.
7. Anti-VISTA gate rule: no pass without screenshot/evidence refs and an executed self-audit.

## Gaps
Cursor and Copilot specifics are secondary-source only; JetBrains Air, llms.txt, Primer, Windsurf, Warp not verified; AGY marketplace.json schema undocumented publicly; Codex loading .claude-plugin formats unverified on a primary page; GPT-6 multi-hour autonomy figures are vendor claims I could not read (openai.com 403).
